                    1                       MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES

                    2   I.     INTRODUCTION

                    3          Together AI, Inc., d/b/a Together Computer, Inc. (“Together”) plans to amend its

                    4   Complaint (Dkt. No. 1) in the above-captioned matter to add specific factual allegations and claims

                    5   related to arguments raised in Defendants Sesterce France Labs SAS’s (“Sesterce France Labs”)

                    6   and Sesterce Group SAS’s (“Sesterce Group”) (collectively with Sesterce France Labs, “Sesterce”

                    7   or “Defendants”) October 6, 2025 Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 25). Given that the Motion to

                    8   Dismiss was filed just this past Monday, October 6, and the deadline for amending pleadings under

                    9   the Court’s Scheduling Order (Dkt. No. 24) is currently set for tomorrow, October 10, Together

                10      respectfully requests that the Court grant this Motion to Modify the Scheduling Order and for

                11      Leave to File a First Amended Complaint (“Motion”) and reset the deadline for amending

                12      pleadings to November 3, 2025. Together has conferred with Defendants, and they do not oppose

                13      this Motion.

                14      II.    STATEMENT OF RELEVANT FACTS

                15             Together filed this lawsuit on June 3, 2025, asserting claims for breach of contract and bad

                16      faith and unfair dealings. (Dkt. No. 1). On September 10, 2025, the Court entered a Scheduling

                17      Order that set an October 10, 2025 deadline to add parties or amend the pleadings, after which a

                18      party may still seek amendment but must demonstrate good cause pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil

                19      Procedure 16(b)(4). (See Dkt. No. 24).

                20             On October 6, 2025, Defendants filed a Motion to Dismiss the Complaint under Federal

                21      Rules of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2) and 12(b)(6) on grounds that Together’s complaint is predicated

                22      on a contract that was “supersed[ed]” by a later version (Dkt. No. 25 at 7), and relatedly, that

                23      Defendants are not proper parties to this dispute (id. at 14-17). Defendants also sought judicial

                24      notice of two versions of the contract at issue in support of their assertions.

                25             On October 8, 2025, two days after Defendants filed their Motion to Dismiss, Together

                26      notified Defendants that it intended to seek leave to amend the Complaint and requested

                27      Defendants’ position on amending the current Case Schedule to allow additional time to amend

                    3   III.    LEGAL STANDARD

                    4          A party’s request to modify a scheduling order is governed by Federal Rule of Civil

                    5   Procedure 16(b)(4), which states that “[a] schedule may be modified only for good cause and with

                    6   the judge’s consent. Coleman v. Quaker Oats Co., 232 F.3d 1271, 1294 (9th Cir. 2000). The good

                    7   cause inquiry under Rule 16(b) “primarily considers the diligence of the party seeking the

                    8   amendment” and “the moving party’s reasons for seeking modification.” Johnson v. Mammoth

                    9   Recreations, Inc., 975 F.2d 604, 609 (9th Cir. 1992). A district court may modify a pretrial

                10      schedule “if it cannot reasonably be met despite the diligence of the party seeking the extension.”

                11      Id. (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 16 advisory committee’s notes (1983 amendment)). It is within a

                12      court’s discretion to modify a scheduling order to permit the filing of an amended complaint based

                13      on an overall evaluation of the “the rights of the parties, the ends of justice and judicial economy.”

                14      U.S. v. Dang, 488 F.3d 1135, 1142 (9th Cir. 2007).

                15             Notwithstanding any applicable deadlines set forth in the scheduling order, amendment of

                16      a complaint is governed by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15. Under that rule, “a party may

                17      amend its pleading once as a matter of course” within 21 days after service of a responsive

                18      pleading. Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1)(B). While further amendments require “the opposing party’s

                19      written consent or the court’s leave,” courts are to “freely give leave [to amend] when justice so

                20      requires.” Id. at 15(a)(2). The Ninth Circuit has similarly held that “leave to amend should be

                21      granted with extreme liberality.” Peterson v. Boeing Co., 715 F.3d 276, 282 (9th Cir. 2013). A

                22      court considers five factors in deciding a motion for leave to amend: bad faith, undue delay,

                23      prejudice to the opposing party, futility of amendment, and whether the plaintiff has previously

                24      amended its complaint. In re W. States Wholesale Nat. Gas Antitrust Litig., 715 F.3d 716, 738

                25      (9th Cir. 2013). Courts determine whether to grant leave “with all inferences in favor of granting

                26      the motion.” Griggs v. Pace Am. Grp., Inc., 170 F.3d 877, 880 (9th Cir. 1999).

                    1   IV.    ARGUMENT

                    2          A.      Good Cause Exists for Together to Amend its Complaint

                    3          Good cause exists under Rule 16(b)(4) to modify the current Case Schedule to provide

                    4   Together time to amend the Complaint. Courts in this Circuit typically find “good cause” to

                    5   modify a case schedule in order to permit amendment of pleadings where, as here, the request for

                    6   leave to amend is made in response to a dispositive motion, such as a motion to dismiss or motion

                    7   for summary judgment, and the factual developments justifying amendment became evident only

                    8   upon the filing of the dispositive motion. See e.g., Iovance Biotherapeutics, Inc. v. Fed. Ins. Co.,

                    9   2025 WL 2426830, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 22, 2025); Miller v. Arizona Beverages USA LLC, 2024

                10      WL 1090627, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 1, 2024) (finding good cause where plaintiff sought leave to

                11      amend in response to defendant filing a motion to dismiss). That is precisely the situation here.

                12      Defendants filed their Motion to Dismiss last Monday, October 6, 2025, just four days before the

                13      deadline to amend the pleadings under the Scheduling Order. Together seeks to amend its

                14      complaint in light of the arguments made in the Motion to Dismiss to clarify and add allegations

                15      and claims in response to that motion. And, but for the October 10 deadline to amend pleadings,

                16      Together would be able to amend the Complaint “as a matter of course” under Rule 15(a)(1)(B).

                17      Together informed Defendants that it intended to seek leave to amend the Complaint two days

                18      after the Motion to Dismiss was filed and filed this Motion one day later. See Entangled Media,

                19      LLC v. Dropbox Inc., 348 F.R.D. 649, 655 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (finding good cause to exist where

                20      party sought amendment soon after discovering the basis for the amendment).

                21             Together has well demonstrated the requisite diligence needed to support a finding of good

                22      cause, and courts routinely grant leave to amend under similar circumstances in recognition that

                23      “[a]dopting a contrary approach would encourage defendants to delay filing their pleadings

                24      motions until after the amended pleadings deadline, thereby undermining the Courts’ ability to

                25      ensure that the pleadings are settled early in the case.” Iovance, 2025 WL 2426830 at *1. For

                26      instance, the Iovance court granted the plaintiff leave to amend after it discovered “specific issues

                27      to be corrected” after reviewing the Defendants’ motion for judgment on the pleadings. 2025 WL

                28      2426830 at *1. And in Miller, the court permitted the plaintiff to amend his complaint two days

                    3   timeliness requirements; and (4) diligently pursued amendment. 2024 WL 1090627, at *1-2.

                    4           As in Miller and Iovance, Together has diligently pursued amendment, has not previously

                    5   amended its Complaint, and seeks leave to amend in direct response to arguments presented in

                    6   Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss regarding key events underlying this litigation. Good cause thus

                    8           B.     A Modest Extension Beyond the Rule 15(a) Deadline is Warranted

                    9           Subject to the Court finding good cause to modify the scheduling order, Together

                10      respectfully requests leave to amend by Monday, November 3, 2025, which is 28 days after the

                11      filing of Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a), “[a] party

                12      may amend its pleading once as a matter course no later than . . . 21 days after service of a motion

                13      under Rule 12(b).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(1)(B). Together seeks a modest 7-day extension of the

                14      otherwise applicable 21-day deadline under Rule 15(a)—which would fall on October 27, 2025—

                15      until November 3, 2025, to ensure that Together has adequate time to conduct a reasonable inquiry

                16      into the factual basis for its amended pleadings. Together has not previously amended its

                17      Complaint, has acted with haste to file this Motion without delay after receiving Defendants’

                18      Motion to Dismiss and analyzing its arguments, and does not request any other adjustments to the

                19      Case Schedule at this time. Considering the deadlines for amendment in Rule 15(a)(1)(b), the

                20      reasons Together seeks extension of the deadline for amending the Complaint, and that the overall

                21      case schedule will not be impacted, the requested extension of time is appropriate.

                22         V.        CONCLUSION

                24      modify the Scheduling Order, and grant Together leave to amend its Complaint on or before

 6 III.      LEGAL ARGUMENT

 7           A.     Legal Standard for Rule 12(b)(6) and 12(f) Motions

 8           A complaint must contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader

 9 is entitled to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a). Dismissal under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6)
10 “is appropriate only where the complaint lacks a cognizable legal theory or sufficient facts to support
11 a cognizable legal theory.” Mendiondo v. Centinela Hosp. Med. Ctr., 521 F.3d 1097, 1104 (9th Cir.
12 2008). “To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted
13 as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678
14 (2009) (quotation marks and citation omitted). “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff
15 pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is
16 liable for the misconduct alleged.” Id. In determining whether a plaintiff has met this standard, the
17 Court must “accept all factual allegations in the complaint as true and construe the pleadings in the
18 light most favorable” to the plaintiff. Knievel v. ESPN, 393 F.3d 1068, 1072 (9th Cir. 2005).
19           However, “[t]he court need not, and does not, accord an assumption of truthfulness to legal

20 conclusions that are not supported by factual allegations in the Complaint or that are contradicted
21 by documents referred to in the Complaint.” Colony Cove Props., LLC v. City Of Carson, 640
22 F.3d 948, 957 (9th Cir. 2011) (emphasis added); see also Williams v. Resler, 2018 WL 4063518, at
23 *3 (S.D. Cal. Aug. 24, 2018) (“[W]hen a court in this circuit weighs contradictory exhibits against
24 allegations in a complaint, a court may deviate from the presumed truthfulness of an allegation by
25 exercising its reasoned judgment and ‘drawing on its judicial experience and common sense.’”)
26 (quoting Ashcroft, supra, 556 U.S. at 679). Similar principles apply under California law in the
27 state court setting, where courts accept as true facts appearing in the exhibits attached to the
28 complaint, although if the facts in the exhibits contradict the facts in the complaint, the facts stated
